Series::nan_to_num¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::nan_to_num(double nan, double posinf, double neginf) const -> Series
Series& Series::nan_to_num_(double nan, double posinf, double neginf)

What It Does¶

nan_to_num() repairs numerically problematic lanes by replacing nan, positive infinity, and negative infinity with ordinary numeric fallbacks that you choose explicitly.

Finite values pass through unchanged. Only the exceptional lanes are rewritten.

This is one of the most practical cleanup surfaces in Series because it lets you say, in one call, what should happen to each problematic numeric state.

Parameters¶

nan (double)

Replacement value for every nan lane.

posinf (double)

Replacement value for every positive-infinity lane.

neginf (double)

Replacement value for every negative-infinity lane.

The three toggles are independent. That matters because many projects want different semantics for “missing”, “overflowed positively”, and “overflowed negatively”.

Returns¶

Series A new Series with the same shape as self, but with exceptional numeric states repaired according to the three replacement parameters.

In-Place Form¶

nan_to_num_() is the in-place sibling of nan_to_num(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

auto x = pluss::make_series({std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(), std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity(), -std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity()});
x.nan_to_num_(0.0, 1e9, -1e9);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1e+09, -1e+09]

Examples¶

Example 1. Each problematic numeric state can be mapped to its own explicit replacement.

auto special = pluss::make_series({
    -std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity(),
    -1.0,
    std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(),
    0.0,
    std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity(),
});

std::cout << special.nan_to_num(0.0, 99.0, -99.0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-99, -1, 0, 0, 99]

The replacement map in that example is:

  • nan -> 0

  • +inf -> 99

  • -inf -> -99

Finite lanes like -1 and 0 survive untouched.

Example 2. The same repair logic applies elementwise across matrices.

auto messy = pluss::make_series({
    {std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(), 1.5, std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity()},
    {-std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity(), -2.5, 0.0},
});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, messy.nan_to_num(-7.0, 500.0, -500.0));

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[-7, 1.5, 500],
  [-500, -2.5, 0]]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • nan_to_num() does not touch already-finite values.

  • The three replacement parameters are positional, so keep their roles straight: nan, then posinf, then neginf.

  • This is a cleanup transform, not a diagnostic mask. If you need detection first, use isnan(), isinf(), or isfinite().

Summary¶

Use nan_to_num() when unstable numeric states should be turned back into explicit finite policy values before the next stage of computation.

See Also¶

  • Series::isnan: detect nan before replacing it.

  • Series::isinf: detect infinities specifically.

  • Series::isfinite: broad finite/non-finite detector.
